summary: Abe Beame argues in Polygon that Martin Scorsese's 21st-century output, culminating in Killers of the Flower Moon, refutes Quentin Tarantino's claim that directors do not get better with age. Scorsese's nine films since 2000 both revisit and revise his old themes and try radical new genres, aided by his partnership with Leonardo DiCaprio and greater creative autonomy. The piece sees Killers as a Catholic reckoning with white supremacy in which Scorsese places himself in the frame.
one_line: Polygon argues Martin Scorsese's nine 21st-century films, up to Killers of the Flower Moon, disprove Tarantino's claim that directors stop improving late in life.
key_facts: In 2021, Quentin Tarantino defended making "just" 10 movies and retiring, saying "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better."
Scorsese had made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; at age 80, Killers of the Flower Moon is his 27th.
Scorsese's nine 21st-century narrative features are Gangs of New York, The Aviator, The Departed, Shutter Island, Hugo, The Wolf of Wall Street, Silence, The Irishman and Killers of the Flower Moon.
The article considers Scorsese's peak run to still be 1976's Taxi Driver through 1990's Goodfellas.
Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio have made six films together over 21 years; the first five are Scorsese's five highest-grossing films.
Scorsese and DiCaprio share a manager, Rick Yorn, who discovered DiCaprio.
Scorsese reimagined Killers of the Flower Moon after DiCaprio gave notes on an early script draft, shifting focus to a different main character and moving DiCaprio into that role.
The Departed was constantly rewritten with the actors on the fly, and Scorsese and editor Thelma Schoonmaker shaped it into a coherent film.
The Aviator (2004) is described as Scorsese's most conventional movie, a director-for-hire palate-cleanser after the troubled Gangs of New York.
Hugo (2011) is a 3D family film and love letter to Georges Méliès, Harold Lloyd and Scorsese's then-12-year-old daughter Francesca.
Killers of the Flower Moon adapts David Grann's book, is Scorsese's first true Western, and centers on a peripheral character from the book.
At an Oct. 16 press conference Scorsese called Killers "a story of complicity, a story of sin by omission," and he appears in the film's closing minutes.
Gangs of New York was the product of a flawed compromise between Scorsese and producer Harvey Weinstein.
